summerstyle10:
Golf style used to mean one thing: logo polo, pleated khakis, visor from the pro shop. That era is over. These ten golfers — tour pros, brand founders, content creators — are actually pushing the look forward. Anthony Kim's comeback wardrobe. Charley Hull's zero-effort cool. Stephen Malbon building an empire. Sam Jones documenting the whole movement as @thegolffashionguy.

What connects them isn't a single aesthetic. It's intention. They think about what they wear the same way they think about their setup. Ryan Peake blends athletic and editorial. Adam Scott keeps it minimal. Kieran Hall treats every round like a lookbook. Golf style has a roster now, and this is the starting lineup.
techbottoms12:
Technical fabrics used to mean shiny, plasticky pants that looked like you got dressed inside a sporting goods store. Not anymore. This is 12 bottoms — shorts and trousers — built from ripstop, Cordura, and performance blends that actually feel like clothes you'd choose to wear.

The range runs from Vuori's $74 Ripstop Short to Outlier's $240 Futureslimworks, with Carhartt WIP, Norse Projects, and Goldwin filling the middle. Water When Dry's Camper Short belongs on a muni or a hiking trail. 686's Everywhere Ripstop Pant lives up to the name. Fantl Sport's AllCourse Pant is engineered in New Zealand and priced like it. Nine brands, zero polyester shame. The course-to-everywhere pant is here, and it doesn't look like golf.
techtops10:
Summer golf in Texas means one thing for your shirt: it better breathe or you're done by the turn. This is 10 technical tops that solve the heat problem without making you look like a catalog mannequin.

Fantl Sport's FutureClassic Polo leads with Sorona renewable fiber and a waterproof zip placket — no buttons, which feels futuristic until you try it. Cotopaxi's Pulso Tech Tee is $55 and punches above its price. Ibex brings merino. Arc'teryx brings Arc'teryx. Carhartt WIP's Chase Pique Polo is the wildcard — a workwear brand making one of the best casual polos for the course. Nine brands, $55 to $108, all built for when the heat index says otherwise.
puttercovers12:
The putter cover market has quietly become one of the most interesting corners of indie golf. Twelve brands, twelve covers, and not a single one looks like it came from the bargain bin at a box store.

Students Golf's Draft Blade is the $50 entry point — clean, magnetic, Texas-made. From there it escalates: Fyfe Golf's Gamekeeper out of Scotland, Gibbons Handmade's Bears Blade, Seamus Golf including a Pendleton collab, and Dormie Workshop's Chevron Atlantic XL at the top. Sunday Rolls, Fried Egg, Winston Collection, Smathers & Branson — all doing their own thing. The common thread is craft. Small-batch, made by people who care about leather, lining, and the snap of a magnetic closure. $50 to $150, all personality.
rangefinder10:
Rangefinders used to be simple: point, click, get a number. Now the category runs from $90 Amazon best-sellers to $600 GPS-laser hybrids, and the gap between cheap and expensive is narrower than the brands want you to think.

The Gogogo Sport Vpro GS24 starts at $90 with 7x magnification, slope mode, and build quality that has no business being that solid at that price. Precision Pro's NX10 Slope and Titan Elite split the middle. Bushnell's Tour V7 Shift is still the tour standard. Garmin's Approach Z82 at $600 combines laser with GPS on a CourseView map — overkill for most, undeniably cool. Ten options, eight brands, every budget covered.
worldcup10:
The 2026 World Cup is coming to Austin, and the city is already planning where to watch. If you play nine in the morning and watch the match in the afternoon, this is your cheat sheet.

Haymaker is the obvious pick — American Outlaws HQ, 40+ taps, garage-door layout on Manor Road. Arrive early or don't bother. But the deeper list matters: Scholz Garten is America's oldest beer garden. Parley runs $3.65 drink specials themed by country. Auditorium Shores hosts Austin FC's free outdoor watch parties. Inn Cahoots is the official World Cup hub on East 6th. Ten spots, from soccer temples to beer gardens to the kind of patio where nobody judges your post-round outfit.
teeedit:
Golf retail is flooded with performance polos and quarter zips. Actual tees — the cotton ones you wear — get overlooked. This is 14 from independent brands that treat the graphic tee like it matters.

Gumtree Golf's To Fight A Mockingbird is the headliner: a $60 clap-back after Under Armour lifted elements of their design. Students Golf brings two — Grass Obsession and God Knows — both screen-printed in Texas. Malbon runs the Bermuda line. Agronomy Workshop's heavyweight work shirt at $136 barely qualifies as a tee but absolutely qualifies as a statement. Radry, Found Golf, Manors, Birds of Condor, Sugarloaf Social Club — 11 brands, three continents, $28 to $136. Not a dri-fit in sight.
sscbyrdie:
Sugarloaf Social Club and Byrdie Golf went to the Bahamas, shot a lookbook, and came back with a nine-piece collab that blurs the line between resort wear and golf gear. The whole collection is built around terry cloth — Cabana Shirt, Anorak, Short, and Mini Skirt, all in bottle green and sand stripes.

The Sugar-Loafer Suede Boat Shoe at $180 is either a golf shoe or a boat shoe depending on your commitment to the bit. A Tour Tote, Tour Towel, seersucker hat, and terry visor round it out. $40 to $180. Camp collar energy, Caribbean color palette, and the distinct feeling that the 19th hole starts at the first tee.
nikes10:
Nike's golf lineup right now is the deepest it's been in years. The Pegasus 1 G — their legendary running shoe, finally adapted for golf — dropped in May 2026 and immediately became the conversation. Hybrid traction, ReactX foam, waterproof. The shoe everyone wondered why it took so long.

But it's not just the Pegasus. The Air Max 90 G is still the crossover king. Jordan's AJ1 Low Golf comes in Chicago and Bred spiked versions at $175. Eastside Golf's AM Plus G "Take Flight" collab adds cultural weight. The C1TY line gives you the sub-$120 spikeless option. Ten shoes, $105 to $275, from the Swoosh family that's finally taking golf as seriously as the culture demands.
walkerpartec:
Walker Golf makes things for the course and the pub. That's their whole philosophy and the Par-Tec drop proves it. Ten pieces in a proprietary lightweight fabric engineered for movement, moisture-wicking, and temperature regulation — but nothing here screams "performance gear."

The Knockout V Polo in Maple is the newest addition and the standout: a V-neck knit collar that reads more European café than American pro shop. The Quarter Zip Fleece in Forest is the layering piece for morning tee times. Members Polo, Kooka Terry Polo, Featherlite Kooka — Walker keeps iterating on the polo silhouette without repeating itself. Shorts and pants in the $90-$100 range, caps at $55. An Australian brand that understands comfort doesn't have to look comfortable.
foundgolf:
Melbourne's Found Golf treats the course like a studio and the dress code like a memo it never received. Fashion-first golf from a city that already knows how to blend streetwear with fine art.

The Box Par Tee is the entry point — a heavyweight graphic shirt that reads like an art-school print, not tournament merch. The Daisy Chain Tee runs the same energy. The Reusable Ciggie Box is actually a tee holder, which is the most Found Golf thing imaginable. Dad cap in olive and The Shiz Vest round out a tight five-piece lineup. Everything priced in AUD, shipped from Australia, but the aesthetic is universal: golf gear for people who went to art school.
drivers12:
Every major OEM dropped a new driver for 2026 and the technology war has never been tighter. Twelve sticks, eight brands, and a price range that runs from $500 to $5,500 if you're feeling unhinged.

TaylorMade's Qi4D leads — ranked #1 across multiple independent tests, Scottie Scheffler's gamer, and the most balanced driver in the field. Callaway's Quantum Triple Diamond Max and Titleist's GTS4 are right behind. PING and Mizuno hold the $500-$600 middle. Then there's the Honma Beres 09 5-Star at $5,500 — a driver that costs more than some memberships. Krank Golf rounds it out for the long-drive crowd. Best year for drivers in a decade, and the hardest year to pick one.
grips7:
Your grip is the only point of contact between you and the club, and most golfers haven't thought about theirs since the day their irons arrived. These seven brands are making grips that are actually interesting to look at.

RIPIT Grips leads from Queensland — 14 designs including artist collabs with Evan Weselmann and Nori Okawa, natural rubber, weather-resistant. Loudmouth and TourMARK did a Magic Bus set. Stinger Grips has a Lavender Lemonade colorway. Sweet Rollz made a Muertos putter grip. IOMIC offers custom color builds. Gimme Grips does florals. And Golf Pride's Honorary Starter Tour Velvet proves even the biggest name in grips can still do something special. $8 to $60.
shinnecock6:
The U.S. Open heads to Shinnecock Hills and the capsule collections are already lining up. Six brands, six takes on America's oldest incorporated golf club — from heritage knitwear to limited-edition rope hats.

J.Lindeberg's 30th anniversary capsule pays tribute to Jesper Parnevik's 1998 Open look — pink trousers, black sweater, iconic snapback, reimagined in polos and pleated pants. Hovland and Norgaard will wear it at Shinnecock. Peter Millar rolls out the official 126th U.S. Open collection. Greyson's Wolf Flag Rope Hat will sell out first. Smathers & Branson brings needlepoint. Walter Hagen and adidas Golf round it out. $45 to $300+, all dropping before the first tee shot.
lionsmuny:
Lions Municipal Golf Course opened in 1924. It was Austin's first public course. In 1950, it quietly became the first desegregated public course south of the Mason-Dixon line. Now it's getting the renovation it deserves.

Coore & Crenshaw — the same architects behind Sand Valley and Streamsong — are doing the restoration, and they're doing it for free. New clubhouse. A teaching center. Trails connecting the course to Town Lake. This isn't a tear-down. It's a revival of a course that helped shape Austin's relationship with public golf. Ben Crenshaw learned the game here. So did Tom Kite. The bones of Lions Muny have always been there. The city is finally investing in making sure they last another hundred years.
mogshade:
Mogshade makes headcovers by hand in Portugal from deadstock fabrics rescued from wool factories in the Serra da Estrela mountains. Every piece is slightly different because the fabric isn't mass-produced — what you get is what's left from the loom.

The Estate Headcover is the flagship at $85 — fleece-lined, leather-detailed, the kind of thing that starts conversations before you reach the first tee. The Azulejo pulls from Portuguese tilework. The Churra Mono at $100 is the premium play. The Parmore collab is limited to 50 pieces. And the Contour Golf Towel at $47 proves the brand can do more than covers. Ten pieces, all handcrafted, all carrying that texture you only get from fabrics with a history.
wwdgarden:
Water When Dry is built on a garden metaphor — what you water will grow — and somehow it's not annoying. Colorways named River, Dusk, Leaf, Soil, Blackberry. Membership called the Garden Club. It should tip into self-help territory, but the clothes are too good for that.

The Camper Short at $88 is the entry point and the piece that shows up in every TGI roundup for a reason. Canopy Zip Hoodie in Leaf and Charcoal. Canopy Fleece in Blackberry for cold mornings. The April Showers Tee and Greener Grass Tee bring graphic energy without trying too hard. $15 to $128, a tight product range, and a brand voice that's wholesome without being corny. Harder than it sounds.
masters27:
Augusta National opened the 2027 Masters ticket application and you have twenty days. The window runs June 1-20 at masters.com. No extensions, no reminders, no second chances.

Roughly two million people will apply. About 0.55% will get in. The rest will refresh their email for three months, convince themselves the notification went to spam, and then quietly look up practice round badges from a guy named Todd. If you've never applied: fill out the form, forget about it, let hope do its work through the fall. If you have applied and never gotten picked, welcome to the club with more members than Augusta. June 20. Hope accordingly.
bottles11:
Hydration on the course is not optional — especially in Texas, especially in summer, especially when you're walking. These 11 water bottles are the ones we'd actually clip to a bag or carry in a cart.

Sentinel Golf leads with the Basecamp — ultralight titanium, single-wall, handcrafted with the same attention they put into their headcovers. $68. Gumtree Golf has two Nalgene collabs in the $46 range. Malbon did a Stanley ProTour Tumbler. Manors, Quiet Golf, and Kinto keep it clean. The Owala FreeSip at $28 is the sleeper — the mainstream bottle golfers are quietly adopting because the sip-or-swig lid works with one hand. Titanium craft to everyday carry, $28 to $72.
burgers12:
You just played 18 in the Austin heat. You need a burger. Not a fancy one with truffle aioli and a brioche bun that falls apart — a proper burger from a place that takes the patty seriously.

Sour Duck Market's Wagyu double smash is the pick: Peeler Farms wagyu, crispy edges, American and pimento cheese, on the best challah bun in East Austin. $14. NADC Burger on Rainey rivals it. Carpenters Hall is the sleeper. LeRoy and Lewis smokes their brisket burger. Casino El Camino's Amarillo Burger has been settling arguments for decades. P. Terry's is the no-debate post-round default. Ten burgers, ten neighborhoods, zero bad options.
munikids10:
Before "indie golf" was a hashtag, Muni Kids was already in the trenches. Brothers Maxton and Drew Reinland started the brand in Portland in 2015 with a simple premise: make gear for the people who learned the game on public courses, not the ones with legacy memberships. Eleven years later, they've built an entire world around that idea — headcovers, apparel, art, a podcast, urban golf meetups, a children's book called Golforia, and a brick-and-mortar shop inside Portland's Memory Den.

This is the brand that proved muni golf had a culture before anyone thought to monetize it. The price range sits at $30 to $85, the aesthetic leans screen-printed and hand-drawn, and the whole operation still feels like it's run by two guys who'd rather be walking nine holes than taking a meeting. If you've been looking for the origin story of this whole movement, it starts here.
hats14:
The hat game in indie golf right now is absurd in the best way. Fourteen picks, fourteen brands, and not a single logo you'd find in a corporate pro shop. We pulled from art-driven studios, small-batch makers, and the kind of labels that treat a rope cap like a canvas.

Radry's mid-crown number splits the difference between dad hat and structured cap with Tony Knapton's hand-drawn graphics doing all the talking. From there it fans out — brands that treat headwear like their flagship product, not an afterthought. Price range sits between $35 and $65, which means you can grab two or three without losing sleep. If your hat rotation is still all tour logos and freebies from demo days, this is the reset.
manorsgj:
Manors teamed up with Gentleman Jack to do something that sounds like a stretch on paper but lands perfectly on the hanger. The entire capsule pulls its paisley print from engraved detailing on vintage Gentleman Jack bottles, and the fabric story is just as considered — Seawool made from recycled oyster shells and plastic bottles, UV 50+ protection, four-way stretch throughout.

The range runs $21 to $283, covering everything from course-ready pieces to the kind of lifestyle gear that plays equally well at a whiskey tasting or a Saturday morning tee time. Manors keeps proving they can do collabs without diluting their identity, and this one might be their most interesting yet. Whiskey branding on golf apparel shouldn't work. It does.
malbongallo:
Malbon's summer drop channels the Gallo Colorido — Portugal's iconic painted rooster — and the whole collection carries that Mediterranean warmth. Lightweight nylon-spandex windshirts, partial zips, high collars, and a color palette that runs through Chive, Surf Spray, and Cream. Every piece says coastal resort without the try-hard energy.

The construction is built for the reality of summer golf: transitional conditions, marine layers that burn off mid-round, and mornings that start cool and end sticky. Prices run $45 to $168, keeping it accessible for a brand that often pushes higher. This is Malbon doing what they do best — taking a cultural reference point and making it feel natural on the first tee.
specialday:
Every golfer in Austin has their regular muni rotation, but sometimes you need something bigger. A birthday round. An anniversary. A Tuesday where you just need to feel like you're on vacation. This is the list for that — eight courses within driving distance of Austin that justify the splurge and the extra hour in the car.

Wolfdancer Golf Club out in Lost Pines leads the pack — Arthur Hills carved it through the property like he had personal beef with flat terrain, and the closing stretch from 14 to 18 is one of the best in Texas. Fazio Canyons at Barton Creek, Ram Rock at Horseshoe Bay, and the underrated Vaaler Creek in Blanco round out the top. Green fees run from $52 at Falconhead to $275 at Barton Creek, so there's something here whether you're treating yourself or going all in.
hoodies14:
Fourteen hoodies from twelve brands, and every single one was designed by people who actually play golf. This isn't the fleece wall at your local sporting goods store. It's the intersection of streetwear weight, course-ready cuts, and the kind of graphics that make you look like you know something the rest of the foursome doesn't.

Eastside Golf's Core Fleece Swingman sets the tone at ~$88 — premium cotton, Swingman embroidery, streetwear DNA. From there, Gumtree Golf goes heavyweight at $145, Malbon pushes into the $185 range with the Safety Buckets Fesque, and Casualist keeps it understated at ~$85. Brands like Sounder, Sugarloaf Social Club, and Jones Golf Bags fill the middle. Whether you need a layer for early morning tee times or a post-round pullover that doesn't scream "I just played 18," the edit covers it.
golfbooks7:
Seven books. No gimmicks. These are the ones that keep showing up on the nightstands of golfers who actually get better — the titles your teaching pro has read twice and your playing partner quotes on the back nine without realizing it.

Ben Hogan's Five Lessons is the foundation. Harvey Penick's Little Red Book is the soul. Rotella's Golf is Not a Game of Perfect rewires your mental game, and Zen Golf by Dr. Joseph Parent takes it deeper. Pelz's Short Game Bible is the technical manual for everyone losing strokes inside 100 yards. Nilsson and Marriott's Every Shot Must Have a Purpose connects the dots between practice and play. All under $17 each. The cheapest equipment upgrade you'll ever make.
putters26:
The 2026 putter market is stacked. Eight new flatsticks from eight different makers, and the technology gap between the big names and the boutique shops has never been smaller. L.A.B. Golf's LINK.2.1 brings Lie Angle Balance to a traditional blade at $599. Scotty Cameron's Phantom 5 and Bettinardi's BB1 hold the heritage lane. Toulon Design's Austin H1 — yes, named after our city — sits at $600.

Mizuno's M.Craft City Series at $350 is the value play. Swag Golf's Handsome One at $400 is the culture play. Evnroll's ER2 Origin and LA Golf's Bel-Air X round out a lineup where every option has a real argument behind it. If you've been rolling with the same putter since 2019, this is the year that changes.
radrygolf:
Tony Knapton runs Radry Golf out of Sheboygan, Wisconsin, and the brand is exactly what happens when an artist decides golf gear is his medium. Every hat, crewneck, and headcover starts as one of Tony's illustrations — hand-drawn, art-school energy, zero corporate polish. The smiley-face logo is becoming one of the most recognizable marks in independent golf, and the brand's gallery arm through White Dot Market sells signed prints alongside $42 dad hats.

The lineup runs from Custodian Hats and Dive Team caps at $42 up through the Contrast Quarter Zip at $120, with the Bugging Blade Cover ($65) and Smoke Em' Ashtray ($55) filling in the weird-in-a-good-way accessories lane. Collabs with Seamus add credibility, but Radry doesn't need borrowed clout. This is a brand that treats golf like a canvas, and the canvas keeps getting bigger.
accessories:
Six accessories from six different brands, and none of them came from a pro shop impulse rack. This is the edit for golfers who care about the small stuff — the brush clipped to your bag, the headcover protecting your putter, the water bottle that actually looks good sitting in your cup holder.

Dimple & Divot's Murphy Hickory Brush ($45) is handcrafted in Raleigh with American hickory and nylon bristles. Sentinel Golf's Basecamp Water Bottle ($68) is titanium and built to last longer than your swing changes. Depeche Golf contributes Issue #4 of their print magazine, Mogshade brings a Portuguese-made headcover, Walker Golf adds a ball marker three-pack, and Jones rounds it out with the Ranger Cooler. Different countries, different categories, same idea: the details matter.
munigrub:
Austin has five public golf courses and the on-course food situation at each one tells a very different story. We ranked every food spot across the muni system — from vending machines to full-service cantinas — so you know exactly what you're walking into before you tee it up.

Fairways Cantina at Morris Williams takes the crown. Cisco's Muny Cafe at Lions Municipal is a close second — the kind of no-frills counter that's been fueling rounds since before most of us were born. Stag & Finch at Jimmy Clay/Roy Kizer holds down third, and Hancock's clubhouse window rounds out the list with vending-machine vibes redeemed by the neighborhood restaurants nearby. If you're choosing your muni based on the course alone, you're only getting half the picture.
merrillgolf:
Merrill Golf calls itself a design venture through the lens of golf, and that's not marketing language — it's a literal description of how the brand operates. No polos. No moisture-wicking polyester. Instead: acid-washed tees, heavyweight hoodies, five-panel caps, and a flying-duck logo that channels vintage Americana more than any country club.

The Target Practice Tee ($60) and Golf Company Tee ($55) are the entry points — graphic-heavy, built on premium blanks, designed to be worn as much off the course as on it. The Birds Dad Hat ($50) and Target Practice Zip Hoodie ($150) round out a tight catalog that feels more tackle shop than fairway. Merrill is making golf apparel for people who fish, hunt, and happen to play golf — and it turns out that audience is bigger than anyone expected.
golfbags:
Seven bags from six brands, and every one of them was designed by people who think your bag should look as considered as the rest of your kit. This is not a roundup of whatever's on sale at the big-box stores. This is the short list for golfers who treat their bag like the centerpiece it is.

Jones leads with the 2026 Trouper 4.0 ($315) and the Heritage Trouper ($375) — two different takes on the same obsessive design philosophy. MacKenzie's 8-inch Waxed Canvas Mac ($740) is the heirloom play. Vessel's Lux Stand ($399), Stitch's SL2 Gen 2 ($398), and Shapland's Kantle 3.1 ($490) hold the premium middle. Ghost Golf's Anyday Kovert Ops ($415) rounds it out with a tactical edge. These are the bags people notice on the first tee.
metalwoodss26:
Metalwood Studio's SS26 collection is ten pieces deep and every single one looks like it was designed by someone who grew up on skate graphics and indie zines. The Double Plaid Windbreaker ($288) is the headliner — full patchwork in a relaxed cut that's loud enough for the first tee and light enough for the bar after. The adidas x Metalwood MC70 Golf Shoe ($200) anchors the footwear side of the collab.

In between, the King of the Greens Jersey ($168) and Micro Grid Button Up ($168) handle the technical-but-stylish lane, while the Digital Hombre Top and Short ($154/$136) push the pattern work into new territory. Hats at $48 and $58 keep the entry point accessible. Metalwood keeps doing what nobody else in golf is willing to try, and SS26 might be their most confident collection yet.
sentinel1733:
Sentinel Golf linked up with Chicago bag maker 1733 on a capsule built around Saltex — a triple-layer Japanese nylon that's salt-bath heat-treated for a dense, organic texture you won't find anywhere else in golf. The material is the story: rigid out of the box, softens with humidity, snaps back when it dries. DWR coated throughout.

The lineup covers a shoe bag ($138), tote ($320), and duffle ($320), all in Saltex Charcoal. Sentinel also dropped the V4 Bag Brush in Olive ($128) alongside the collab pieces. Everything is made in Chicago, everything is limited, and the material process alone justifies the price tags. Two brands that obsess over craft, working in a fabric that most golf brands wouldn't even know how to source.
casualist:
Casualist and Walker Golf share this double feature, and together they paint a picture of where indie golf apparel is headed — elevated basics, earthy palettes, and the kind of restraint that lets the fabric do the talking. Casualist's side runs from the All The Gear Sweatshirt ($140) and Cart Path Ripstop Jacket ($339) down to a $21 ball marker, covering polos, trousers, tees, and caps in muted tones that look good against any course backdrop.

Walker Golf fills the second half with Australian-rooted pieces — the Jersey Knit Sweater, Kookaburra Quilted Vest, and a Walker x adidas Ultimate365 Jacquard Polo at $100. Both brands share a philosophy: make things that work on the course and still look right at the pub after. No neon. No logos you can read from the fairway. Just good clothes for golfers who've outgrown the pro shop.
premtees:
Six golf tees. All of them cost more than the fast-food lunch you grabbed on the way to the course. And somehow, every one of them makes a case for why the upgrade is real.

Flightpath's Diamond Tee ($23 for eight) is polycarbonate, diamond-shaped, and packaged in a matchbox — the aerodynamics pitch actually holds up under testing. Bird Darts went bamboo at $6.99 for 18. Western Birch hand-paints striped birch tees. Lignum machines micro-sized wooden tees in Germany. Green Swing does sustainable bamboo. And Brimz Supply made cigarette-shaped tees called Tee Box Smokes ($12.99 for 10), which is either genius or unhinged depending on your sense of humor. The humble golf tee got interesting when nobody was looking.
boldtees:
Twelve graphic tees from eleven brands, and every one of them says something about who you are on the course without requiring a conversation. This is the roundup for golfers who want their shirts to have a point of view — not a swoosh and a tagline, but actual design intent.

Quiet Golf's Monogram Washed Pocket Tee ($55) leads with tonal subtlety. Random Golf Club's S.F.E. Clubhouse Tee ($40) and Students Golf's Grass Obsession ($52) bring the community energy. Devereux, Manors, Radry, Metalwood Studio, and GGNC fill the middle with graphics that range from cactus art to medieval crests. Kingfisher Golf's Getting Worse Tee ($34.99) is the most honest shirt in the game. Walker Golf and Merrill Golf close it out. Prices run $34.99 to $62 — low enough to stock up, high enough that the blanks are actually good.
19thhole:
The round is over. The sun is dropping. You're sunburned, slightly dehydrated, and not ready to go home. Austin has you covered.

Five spots, five different vibes, all designed for the golfer who treats the 19th hole like the most important one. Equipment Room at Hotel Magdalena on Music Lane brings the craft-cocktail-and-vinyl energy. Only The Wild Ones on South Congress is the patio hang. Frazier's Long & Low on the South Shore keeps it low-key. Domo Alley-Gato on East 6th is the outdoor bar with games and tacos. And The Golden Horn on North Loop is the neighborhood spot where nobody cares that you're still wearing golf shoes. No reservations needed, no dress code enforced, no judgment for ordering a second round before 6 PM.
threeputtround:
European brand 3 Putt Round has one joke and they commit to it completely: golf is an addiction, so the accessories should look like vices. Tees come packaged in cigarette boxes and matchbooks. The branding leans hard into punchy colors, cheeky copy, and the kind of packaging that belongs on a shelf as much as in your bag.

The lineup runs from Golf Tee Matches at 20 euros to the Addiction Knitted Polo at 120 euros, with towels, caps, and various tee packs filling in the middle. The Vecchio x Lost Balls Towel collab adds some crossover credibility. Everything ships from Europe, everything is designed to make your playing partners do a double take when you pull tees out of what looks like a pack of smokes. It's novelty done with enough craft and humor that it actually sticks.
freshpieces:
Twelve brands. Twelve picks. No filler. This is the warm-weather rotation we'd actually wear — a one-from-each pull across the indie golf map. Malbon's SS26 Studio Collection leads the pack, Manors pairs their Course Pullover with the Greenskeeper Trouser, and Public Drip's Frequency Polo collab with Cleeks GC brings the muni energy.

The range here is the point. You've got Whim Golf's $309 merino long sleeve sitting next to Devereux's $74 Back9 Polo, and both make sense. Eastside Golf, Quiet Golf, Birds of Condor, Sugarloaf, Metalwood, Greyson, UNRL — each one doing their own thing, none of them copying each other. Summer sorted.
publicdrip:
Neil Tan rediscovered golf at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx in 2020, and the result is Public Drip — a label built for the golfers who grew up on public courses, not private ones. Brooklyn-based, streetwear-rooted, and already making noise with a Hypebeast feature, a Cleeks GC collab, and a LINKS Magazine nod as one of 2026's brands to watch.

The lineup runs deep: Frequency and Up & Down polos at $100, Anywhere Pleated Pants at $170, Tech Shorts at $90, and a full accessories run with the "P" Script bucket hat, snapback, and putter cover. Nothing here costs more than $170, and everything looks like it came from a brand three times the size. Muni golf has a uniform now.
manorsss26:
Manors keeps building the bridge between the pub and the first tee, and SS26 is their most complete collection yet. Recycled fabrics, organic cotton, earthy colorways — the whole thing feels like a weekend at a British links course, minus the rain. The Jones collab bag at $314 is the standout flex, but the Buttersoft Polo and GOAT Pique Polo at $116 each are where most people will start.

The Greenskeeper Jacket ($218), Highland Pullover ($191), and Course Gilet ($150) give you layering options that don't scream "I'm wearing golf clothes." Club Pant, Ranger Short, Stableford Short — every bottom in the lineup fits the same relaxed ethos. UK streetwear DNA, course-ready construction, no dress code anxiety.
roykizer:
Built on a decommissioned wastewater treatment plant in southeast Austin, Roy Kizer is the muni that shouldn't exist — and it might be the most interesting public course in the city. Named after the man who kept Lions Muny alive as superintendent from 1937 to 1973, the course opened in 1994 and plays like a proper links: 40-plus bunkers, 35 acres of lakes, 22 acres of wetlands, and a par-71 layout stretching 6,749 yards.

Sit it next to its sibling Jimmy Clay — a parkland track sharing the same address — and you've got 36 holes in two completely different styles for $35 weekday, $44 weekend. The GolfATX muni system doesn't get enough credit for what it offers, and Roy Kizer is Exhibit A. Southeast Austin's best-kept secret is hiding in plain sight.
hatstowels:
Six hats. Six towels. Twelve indie brands. No big-box logos in sight. This is the accessory edit for golfers who treat their bag like an outfit — Agronomy Workshop's Work Hat with its built-in pencil holder, Metalwood Studio's Tour Sponsor Strapback, Fiori Golf's Dune 5-Panel, and the Manors Chino Cap holding down the headwear side.

On the towel rack, it's Agronomy's Unusual Lies blueprint print, Dormie Workshop's Player's Towel, the Birds of Condor Coogi-print towel that has no business being that fun, and Cayce Golf's Caddy Towel at $24.99 — the budget entry that punches up. Everything here runs $24.99 to $56. Small details, big personality.
texascourses:
Texas is too big to play one course and call it done. This is the premium ten — the courses you build a weekend around, from desert canyon holes in Big Bend to PGA Tour-grade conditioning in Frisco. Black Jack's Crossing at Lajitas might be the most dramatic tee box in the state. Fields Ranch East and West at PGA Frisco give you two championship layouts in one trip.

Closer to Austin, the Fazio Canyons and Foothills tracks at Barton Creek deliver clifftop golf that rivals anything in the Southwest. TPC San Antonio runs two courses — Oaks and Canyons — both tournament-tested. Wolfdancer at Lost Pines, Horseshoe Bay's Apple Rock, and La Cantera round it out. Green fees run $150 to $330, and every dollar buys conditioning and design you won't find at the muni. Sometimes you need to splurge.
aussiegolf:
Three brands from the other side of the world doing golf apparel better than most of the names you already know. Left of Field Golf leads with the Elements Polo and a relaxed Australian sensibility — Nick Ilias built this brand around landscapes, not dress codes. Walker Golf Things brings the adidas collab Quarter Zip, the Knockout V Polo, and knits that feel like they belong at a coastal links.

Then there's Penta Golf — the Grid Polo collab with Barnaby's in Lemon Sorbet is the kind of piece that starts conversations on the range. Across all three, you're looking at $55 to $296, with most picks landing well under $150. Australia's indie golf scene is real, and these three are leading it.
firecracker:
The Firecracker Open has been running at Lions Municipal every Fourth of July weekend since 1945 — 81 years of amateur golf on Austin's oldest public course. This is the tournament where Crenshaw, Kite, and Uresti all cut their teeth before turning pro. 54 holes, no cut, and a field that mixes college stars with 60-year-old regulars who know every break on every green.

The Muny itself opened in 1924 as nine holes cut through the oaks on Enfield Road. In 1950, it quietly became the first desegregated public course south of the Mason-Dixon line. The Muny Conservancy is overseeing ongoing renovations, including a new 8,000-square-foot putting green. The 2026 Firecracker runs July 3-5. If you've never watched it, this is the year.
sugarloafss26:
Sugarloaf Social Club just dropped SS26 and the collection reads like a country club catalog written by someone who actually has taste. The SSC Anorak at $165 is the hero — water-resistant, packable, and clean enough for a lawn party in Savannah. The Tournament Oxford at $120 is the button-up that works on the course and at dinner after.

Polos run $95 to $105 across solid, club stripe, mini stripe, and long-sleeve options. The Tech Vest at $115 slots in as the mid-layer you'll reach for more than you expect, and the Needlepoint Belt at $195 is the luxury play. Top it off with the Cotton SSC Arrow Cap or the High Crown Visor, both under $42. Georgia roots, no pretension, and a Sun Hoody that proves Sugarloaf isn't just a warm-weather brand.
metalwood:
Metalwood Studio is what happens when skate graphics and indie brand culture crash into golf — and nobody apologizes for it. Based on medieval heraldry and industrial signage, the design language is unlike anything else in the space. The Tri-Metal Tee at $54 is the entry point. The Bomber Jacket at $228 and Mechanic Jacket at $278 are the statement pieces.

The Metalwood x adidas MC70 Golf Shoe at $200 gives the brand a legitimate footwear play alongside polos, pullovers, and hats that range from $44 to $188. The Medieval Terry Polo, the World Class Zip Polo, the Madras Explorer Shirt — every piece looks like it was designed by someone who cares more about art direction than sell-through. That's the whole point, and it's working.
towels:
Twelve towels from twelve brands, and not a single one came from a pro shop bargain bin. The Sugarloaf Social Club SSC Golf Towel leads with a heavy-weight waffle knit and a magnetic clip that actually holds. Gumtree Golf's Member Caddy Towel at $50 is the premium play. Jones Sports Co's Storm Towel matches it. And at the other end, Swannies' Santiago Towel at $25 proves you don't need to spend big to clip something good to your bag.

In between, you've got Walker Golf Things, Random Golf Club's limited Tempo Towel, Birds of Condor, Sunday Golf, Malbon, Ghost Golf's magnetic caddie, Devereux, and Stitch. The spread runs $25 to $50. Small accessory, big personality differentiator.
indoorsims:
Austin's weather is great for golf about 300 days a year. The other 65, you need a backup plan. These seven indoor sim spots cover every vibe — from Southside Golf Co's no-frills TrackMan warehouse in Manchaca to Five Iron Golf's 12-bay downtown location coming later in 2026.

Golfinity in NW Austin runs 22 bays across multiple tech platforms. ROK Golf has Trackman setups on S Lamar and in Bee Cave. ATX Indoor Golf Club brings Trackman iO with 4K projection. X-Golf in Cedar Park adds a sports bar to the equation. And Back Nine Golf covers three locations — SW, East, and Westlake — with 24/7 access for the truly obsessed. Rain check, cancelled.
puttercovers:
Eleven putter covers from eleven brands, and every one of them has more personality than the putter it's protecting. Birds of Condor's Tokyo Country Club blade cover channels Japanese minimalism at $69.95. Dormie Workshop's 3 Wishes Mallet Cover at $155 is handcrafted leather you'll be nervous to actually use. Gumtree Golf's Studio Collection Cover at $120 sits right in the sweet spot of design and price.

Jones Golf Bags, Stitch Golf, Rose & Fire, Fyfe Golf, EP Headcovers, Winston Collection, Cayce Golf, and Sunday Golf round it out — blade covers, mallet covers, leather, canvas, needlepoint, and screen-printed. The $44.99 Sunday Golf Toasted Almond is the quiet sleeper. The spread runs from there to $155, and the only wrong answer is the generic one your driver came with.
whitetees:
It's June in Texas. It's going to be 102 degrees. You need a white tee that breathes, doesn't cling, and doesn't look like you gave up. Ten picks, ten brands, zero polyester existential crises. Devereux's Club Toss Tee is 100% Pima cotton with a scattered club print at $44. Greyson's Falcon Sport SS at $90 is the premium play. Kingfisher Golf's Golfmobile Tee at $30 is the steal.

In between, Manors, Birds of Condor, Barstool Golf, Holderness & Bourne, Eastside Golf, Radry Golf, and Malbon Golf each bring a different take on the same idea: keep it white, keep it clean, keep it moving. The white tee is the most democratic piece of golf clothing that exists. These ten prove it doesn't have to be boring.
malbonseoul:
Malbon's Studio Seoul line is the technical collection the brand has been building toward. This isn't the Buckets-logo-on-a-hoodie play — it's 3-Layer Tech Jackets at $448, Rain Jackets at $428, and a Hybrid Anorak at $318 with insulated body panels and stretchy woven sleeves engineered for rounds where the weather changes every three holes.

The Double-Knit Pullover, Buckets Polo Sweater, and Panelled Mock Neck fill out the mid-layer range from $208 to $368. The Cargo Pant at $288 and Seam-Sealed Bucket Hat at $112 round it out. Everything is built for bad weather and priced like it. Malbon is making a case that golf outerwear can be both technical and designed — not one or the other.
kingfisher:
Fiona started Kingfisher Golf at a kitchen counter in East Dallas with a simple pitch: nice things, fair prices. Polos, tees, and caps — nothing else. Every production run is 100 pieces or fewer. No hype drops, no performance fabric monologues, no lifestyle fiction.

The Kit Polo, Black Striped Polo, and Cream Polo all come in at $49.99. The Worst Golfer in Dallas Tee is $34.99 and might be the most honest piece of golf apparel on the market. The Logo Golfer Cap is $24.99. That's the entire catalog, and that's the point. Made with heart in Texas. If you've been waiting for a golf brand that respects your wallet and your taste, this is the one.
practiceatx:
Eight places to sharpen your game around Austin, from all-grass ranges to Toptracer bays to the most iconic par-3 course in the city. Harvey Penick Golf Campus in East Austin leads the list — all grass, no mats, two putting greens, a practice bunker, a 3-hole short course, and $8-$14 buckets. Named after the man who wrote the Little Red Book. Perpetually underrated.

Avery Ranch brings Toptracer tech in NW Austin. Topgolf at The Domain is the social play. Butler Pitch & Putt in Zilker is the 9-hole par-3 that every Austin golfer should play at least once. Jimmy Clay / Roy Kizer's muni range covers SE Austin, Lions Muny handles central, Dripping Springs CC adds Toptracer out west, and The Driving Range in Round Rock gives you 35 lit acres if you're a north-of-the-river person.
ztputters:
Zero-torque putters are the technology story that's actually changing how people roll the ball. The concept is simple: balance the putter so the face doesn't want to twist during the stroke. The execution is anything but. Five brands are leading the charge, and they're all approaching it differently.

Bettinardi's Hexperimental #7 is a heel-shafted mid-mallet built around the SimplyBalanced system — milled in-house, honeycomb face, pre-sale started in April. Odyssey's S2S Tri-Hot SB, Evnroll's ZERO Z5cs Major Edition, Wilson's Infinite Zero Torque 606, and TaylorMade's Spider ZT each bring their own take. If your putting stroke has a twist problem, the fix might not be lessons — it might be physics.
markerbrands:
The ball marker used to be a quarter or a poker chip from a casino you barely remember. Now it's a whole category. Ten indie brands are making markers that double as collectible art — CNC-milled, hand-painted, limited-run, and occasionally absurd in the best way.

Swag Golf is the king of the drop: bottle caps, NES cartridges, 8-balls, all milled in Atlanta and selling out in minutes. Seamus Golf brings the Arnold Palmer Umbrella marker in copper. Matchstick Golf's Old Fashioned at $20 is the tasteful entry point. Hatch Golf, Doubloon Golf, and Willie's Golf Goods push into the $30-$85 range with designs that belong on a shelf. PRG Golf's Arnold Palmer Ice Tea at $7.50 proves you don't need to spend crazy money to mark your ball with personality.
postroundatx:
You just finished 18. The sun's still up. You're not ready to go home. Austin has seven post-round moves that keep the day going — and none of them require changing out of what you wore on the course.

Paperboy in East Austin handles the early finish with all-day brunch and scratch cocktails. Salt Lick BBQ in Driftwood is the BYOB pit-smoked pilgrimage. Loro on South Lamar is the Aaron Franklin and Tyson Cole Asian smokehouse that makes every other post-round meal feel like an afterthought. Armadillo Den in South Austin, Meanwhile Brewing in SE, Barton Springs Pool in Zilker for a 68-degree cooldown, and Uncommon Objects on South Congress for the golfer who also collects vintage. The round ends. The day doesn't have to.
readthegreen:
Read The Green started as three words shouted at a buddy who missed the pin on a miniature golf course. Four lifelong friends turned that inside joke into a full lifestyle brand — premium hats and apparel that move between the course and the city without trying too hard. Their Founder's Cap is the signature piece, a 5-panel corduroy snapback with embroidered details and a custom interior lining, but the clothing line has taken on a life of its own.

The '97 Vintage Pullover went viral and put RTG on the map — a lightweight nylon layer with rib-knit cuffs and a drawstring waist that works on the back nine or a Saturday morning coffee run. The Grounds Crew Jacket and Oversized Knit Sweater pushed the brand into premium territory, while the Varsity Crewneck and Club Tee keep things accessible. Cody Bellinger, Jasson Domínguez, and Lexie Hull all wear RTG, but the brand still feels like it belongs to the weekend golfer who cares about what they put on. That's the point.
